finding: Round 7 added two rules that cancel each other. §3.1 deletes a role's findings file before each attempt "so a failed attempt's leftovers can never satisfy the next attempt's predicate", but §4.1 makes `next_units` omit any role whose findings file already exists in the round directory. The delete happens at attempt time, after `next_units` was computed, so it only protects an in-run retry. If a role's child writes a partial file and then dies (or the driver dies before the retry), the next `tp run` asks the oracle, the oracle sees the file present, omits the role, and no attempt — and therefore no delete — ever happens. The leftover satisfies the round exactly as before the repair, and the record unit merges it.
suggestion: Name which component owns the freshness decision and state the ordering. Either the driver deletes the file when it *decides to attempt* the unit and the oracle's omission is qualified to files whose attempt is known-complete (e.g. only files the driver marked complete in the round directory), or the oracle's omission is dropped in favour of the driver skipping roles it already ran in this run. Add a test for the cross-run case: a crashed role that left a partial file must be re-run, not skipped.

finding: Test 37 asserts every child receives all eight variables "with their documented forms", including `TP_ROUND_DIR` "derived from phase and round" — but §4.1 says `round` is null outside a round-based phase, and §3.1 defines `TP_ROUND_DIR` only as `.tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND`. For an `implement`, `decompose`, `review-resolve` or `audit-fix` unit the spec never says whether `TP_ROUND`/`TP_ROUND_DIR` are unset, empty, or expanded with a null round (yielding a path ending in `-r`). Two engineers write contradictory assertions for the same test, and the Stop hook (§6.2) and `tp review`/`tp audit` (§6.3) both branch on `TP_ROUND_DIR` being set.
suggestion: State explicitly in §3.1 that `TP_ROUND` and `TP_ROUND_DIR` are unset (not empty) when the oracle reports `round` null, and amend test 37 to assert exactly that for a non-round-based unit.

finding: Round 7's two repairs to the env layer collide on one variable name. §5.1 now says the env layer for a fenced field is `TP_` + the upper-cased field name and is ignored under `TP_UNATTENDED`, and that `runner` "cannot be set at all, at any layer" — that layer is `TP_RUNNER`. §3.2.1 defines `TP_RUNNER` as the test seam that "outranks every layer of §7's precedence, including a CLI flag". Test 40 asserts `runner` is unsettable at any layer under the variable while tests 1, 10 and 11 depend on `TP_RUNNER` winning; children inherit both variables, so no implementation can satisfy both statements for the same name.
suggestion: Separate the seam from the field's env layer: give the seam a name that is not the fenced layer (e.g. `TP_RUNNER_SEAM` / `TP_TEST_RUNNER`), or state explicitly that the seam is evaluated before the unattended fence and that the fence therefore applies to `runner` only at the config/CLI layers. Whichever is chosen, say it in both §3.2.1 and §5.1 and pin it in test 40.

finding: §5.1 fences `runner` "more strictly: ... under the variable a unit cannot set them at all, at any layer" and says the env layer is ignored for every fenced field, whose env name is `TP_` + upper-cased field — which is exactly `TP_RUNNER`. §3.2.1 says `TP_RUNNER` "outranks every layer of §7's precedence, including a CLI flag". Test 1 needs `TP_RUNNER` honoured while test 40 asserts `runner` "cannot be set at any layer" under `TP_UNATTENDED=1`; since the driver sets `TP_UNATTENDED=1` in the same process tree, the two tests assert opposite outcomes for the same variable and neither section says which wins.
suggestion: Pin the interaction in §5.1: either `TP_RUNNER` is exempt from the fence because it is a test seam read by the driver (not by a child's `tp set`), or the fence applies and §3.2.1's "outranks every layer" gets the exception. Then make test 40 name the fenced env vars it checks and exclude `TP_RUNNER` explicitly.

finding: The escalation rule keys on the child's exit code ("A unit that exits 2 having written a record stops the run ...; a unit that exits 2 without one ... is an ordinary unit failure"), but the process the driver spawns is the runner harness, not `tp escalate`. With the shipped `claude` template the child is `claude -p ...`, which exits 0 when the agent session ends normally regardless of what any tool it invoked returned; the same is true of `opencode run`. So the two branches the spec distinguishes ('exit 2 with a record' vs 'exit 2 without one') collapse into 'exit 0 with a record' in the only two configurations that ship, and the driver as specified would treat every escalation as a normal completion. §3.3's "The driver decides a unit succeeded from its exit code and from re-reading cycle state" and §4.2's "When a unit exits non-zero" inherit the same defect.
suggestion: State that the driver's escalation and failure tests are the durable artifacts plus the §3.3 predicate, with the exit code as a secondary signal: an escalation record present for this `(TP_RUN_ID, TP_UNIT_SEQ)` means `escalation` whatever the child returned; a missing predicate with no record means a failed attempt whatever the child returned; and a non-zero exit with the predicate satisfied and no record is still a failed attempt. Say explicitly that a runner is not required to propagate an inner command's exit code, and keep exit-code language out of the escalation rule.

finding: §6.1 requires the plugin to preflight `tp`'s presence and version ("fails with the install command rather than degrading quietly"), but §6.2's hook table is presented as the complete set of shipped hooks and contains no preflight, and the only candidate event is explicitly foreclosed: the SessionStart row's payload is fixed as "`tp resume --compact` and nothing else". Nothing in §6.2, §6.4 or §10.4 gives the preflight an event, a failure channel, or a test, so a required behaviour has no home in the design that must carry it.
suggestion: Either add a fourth row to §6.2's table (e.g. SessionStart runs the version preflight before the orientation injection, with its own 10s timeout per §6.4) and relax the "nothing else" sentence to cover a preflight failure message, or state that the preflight is a plugin-manifest field rather than a hook; add the matching assertion to §10.4.

finding: The dropped-role rule turns on "an input with at least one line, none of which parsed", but the spec never defines what counts as a line for this test. A well-formed NDJSON file ends with a newline, producing a trailing empty line; a file of only blank lines, or one with a comment line, is also "at least one line, none parsed". Test 32 pins only the all-malformed and zero-byte cases, so it cannot separate implementations that count blank lines from ones that skip them — the former makes every trailing-newline file exit 1. The partial case (some lines parse, some do not) is also untested although §8a implies it exits 0 with warnings.
suggestion: Define in §8a that blank/whitespace-only lines are neither parsed nor skipped and never contribute to the exit-1 condition, and add a test row for (a) a valid file with a trailing newline exiting 0, and (b) a file where one of thirteen lines parses exiting 0 with `inputs[].skipped` = 12.

finding: §8a makes `--merge` exit 1 when an input file has lines and none parse, but §3.3's `review-role`/`audit-role` predicate is only that `$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` *exists*, and §6.2's Stop hook stats existence too. A role unit that writes a malformed non-empty file therefore succeeds, while the following record unit fails on every attempt; §3.1 deletes only the *attempted* role's file, and §4.1 says `next_units` "omits any role whose findings file already exists", so no later iteration and no later `tp run` will ever re-run the role that produced the bad file. The round is permanently stuck at `unit-failure` with no supported route back to a good state.
suggestion: Reconcile the two: either make the role predicate "the findings file exists and every line parses" (so the malformed file fails its own unit and is deleted on retry), or state that a `--merge` exit 1 caused by an unparseable input deletes that role's file and returns the role to `next_units`. Add a test to §10.5 covering the malformed-role-file round recovering rather than deadlocking.

finding: Test 5 ("Role units run concurrently and every other kind does not overlap them") and test 6 ("a second `tp run` over the same state resumes at the same unit") have no pinned observable. For test 5 the spec defines no artifact recording overlap — an engineer can assert spawn order, or overlapping wall-clock timestamps from the fake runner (flaky under load, the failure mode CLAUDE.md already records for mutation runs). For test 6, "the same unit" is true only for the `implement` case §3.1 describes; §4.1 and test 45 require a resumed round to omit roles whose findings file already exists, so a crash mid-round resumes at a different set of units.
suggestion: Give the fake runner a concurrency observable the spec names (e.g. a lock-free counter file whose maximum equals the active role count) and assert that maximum; and split test 6 into an `implement` case (same task, resumed `wip`) and a round case (only the roles still missing a findings file).

finding: Test 15 requires four paths to be git-ignored (`.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/`, `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`) while §10.6 says the `.tp/.gitignore` fixture "gains three entries". The counts contradict, and the per-base names are not real gitignore patterns — the fixture assertion cannot be written without knowing whether the entries are `run-*.json`/`last_failure-*.json` globs or something else. Separately, only §3.5 (run state) and §4.2 (`last_failure`) declare git-ignored status in the normative body; no §3-§8a text says `.tp/runs/` or `.tp/rounds/` are ignored, so the test asserts two entries its sections do not require.
suggestion: List the exact `.tp/.gitignore` lines once (e.g. `run-*.json`, `last_failure-*.json`, `runs/`, `rounds/`), state their git-ignored status in §3.1/§3.5 for the two directories, and make §10.6's count match.

finding: Test 26 says the Stop hook "does block one that ended with neither its durable write nor a record", phrased over any unit. §6.2 scopes the hook to `review-role`/`audit-role` only — it fires when `TP_UNIT_KIND` ends in `-role` — and explicitly leaves every other kind's predicate to the driver. An engineer reading test 26 literally writes a case where an `implement` unit with no commit is blocked, which §6.2 forbids; another writes only role cases. Both claim to satisfy the same numbered test.
suggestion: Rewrite test 26 to name the kinds: the hook blocks a `review-role`/`audit-role` unit that wrote neither file, does not block one that wrote an escalation record, and does not fire at all for a non-`-role` `TP_UNIT_KIND`.

finding: Test 31 requires arity violations to exit 2 "for every command, including cobra's own built-ins", but §8a's normative sentence is narrower: "Every command's `Args` validator exits 2". Cobra's generated `help` and `completion` commands do not route their arity errors through tp's `Args` validators, so the test demands behaviour the section does not require and may not be reachable without overriding cobra's own error paths. A tester cannot tell whether a failing `tp completion bogus extra` case is a defect or out of scope.
suggestion: Either extend §8a to state that cobra's built-in commands are wrapped so their arity errors also exit 2, or drop "including cobra's own built-ins" from test 31 and name the command set the rule covers.

finding: Test 36 still asserts "a re-run role overwrites its own file rather than adding one" for the driver-death scenario, but §4.1's round-7 addition makes `next_units` omit any role whose findings file already exists, so in that exact scenario the role is never re-run and the overwrite path is unreachable. Test 36 and test 45 now describe opposite behaviour for the same state.
suggestion: Rewrite test 36's second clause around a role that is legitimately re-attempted (a retry within one run, where §3.1's delete applies) and let test 45 own the resumed-round omission — or, if the leftover-file gap in §3.1 is fixed first, restate 36 in terms of whichever component the fix gives ownership to.

finding: §10.6 says "The `.tp/.gitignore` fixture gains three entries" while test 15 asserts four distinct paths are ignored (`.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/`, `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`), and neither lists `.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock` (§3.1) — a new per-run lock file that would otherwise be committed. Two of the four paths are per-task-file names, so they can only be ignored by a pattern (`run-*.json`, `last_failure-*.json`), which the spec never gives; an implementer writing literal entries produces a fixture that ignores nothing.
suggestion: Give the exact `.tp/.gitignore` lines the release adds — including `locks/` — and make §10.6's count match that list. State the glob form for the per-base files.

finding: §3.1 spawns every child with `TP_ROUND` and `TP_ROUND_DIR`, and derives `TP_ROUND_DIR` as `.tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND`. Round 7's §4.1 now states `round` is null outside a round-based phase, but nothing says what the two variables hold for an `implement`, `decompose` or `review-resolve` unit. The literal derivation yields a path ending in `-r` for a null round; §6.3 makes `tp review`/`tp audit` change their emitted output path whenever `TP_ROUND_DIR` is set, so an empty or malformed value is not inert. Test 37 asserts `TP_ROUND_DIR` is "derived from phase and round" without covering the null case.
suggestion: State that `TP_ROUND` and `TP_ROUND_DIR` are unset (not empty) for children of a unit whose phase has no round, and extend test 37 to assert their absence for a non-round unit and that `tp review`/`tp audit` fall back to the unchanged filename when unset.

finding: How the runner is invoked is never pinned, though §5.2 takes care to pin it for `notify_cmd` ("exec'd without a shell, split on whitespace"). For `runner` the spec does not say whether `cmd`+`args` are exec'd directly or through a shell, nor how placeholders substitute: whether a placeholder must be a whole argument or may appear as a substring (`--prompt={prompt}`), whether one placeholder may appear in several args, and what happens to a `{prompt}` containing newlines and quotes — which it will, since §3.2.1 says the prompt is a multi-clause instruction that embeds the unit's `brief_command`. Under a shell that value needs quoting the spec never specifies; under direct exec it needs none, and the two builds differ for every real prompt.
suggestion: State that `cmd` and `args` are exec'd directly with no shell (matching `notify_cmd`), that each `args` element is substituted textually with no quoting or escaping applied, that a placeholder may appear as a substring and any number of times, and that an unknown `{...}` token is the §3.2.1 usage error.

finding: "Every child is spawned with stdin closed" is a required behaviour carried over from §2's overnight-practice row ("backgrounded runs hang on stdin"), and "Children are spawned in the repository root" (§3.1) is likewise normative — neither has a test anywhere in §10. Test 37 covers only the environment variables. These are precisely the properties whose absence is invisible until an unattended run hangs.
suggestion: Add a test: the fake runner records whether its stdin is closed and its working directory, asserting closed stdin and the repository root for every spawned unit.

finding: Spend reading has no failure path. The driver "reads one number from the final line of that unit's log" via a dot path, but the spec never says what happens when the final line is not JSON, when the dot path is absent or resolves to a non-number, or when the log is empty (a runner that died before writing anything). The three plausible builds differ in outcome: treat the unit's spend as null and continue, fail the attempt, or stop the run — and the choice is load-bearing, because a silently-null spend makes `cap-budget` under-accrue exactly the way §8a says a truncated audit under-reports. §3.2.2 explicitly reports the declared-no-`spend_key` case "once at run start, not silently", which shows the intent but does not cover the unparseable case.
suggestion: Add a row or sentence: a declared `spend_key` that cannot be read from the final line records `spend_usd: null` for that unit, does not fail the attempt, and emits one stderr line naming the unit and log path; state whether such units are also named in the run-start unmetered report or in `--status`.

finding: §3.2.2's per-kind rule — "the cap accrues only the reporting kinds, and the run-start report names which kinds are unmetered" — has no test. Test 11 covers only the single-runner case and asserts a runner without `spend_key` "leaves `cap-budget` inert", which reads as inert for the whole run and contradicts the per-kind case where metered kinds still accrue toward `run_max_budget_usd`. Nothing pins where the run-start report appears (stdout, `--status`, run state) or its shape, so no deterministic assertion can be written for it.
suggestion: Add a test for a per-kind runner map with one unmetered kind: metered units accrue, the unmetered kind reports `spend` null, and the run-start report names the unmetered kinds — and say in §3.2.2 which surface and field carry that report.

finding: "A unit is attempted `1 + run_max_unit_retries` times" never says where a retry happens in §3.1's six-step loop. Two builds are equally consistent with the text: retry inline before step 5 (the driver re-spawns the same unit immediately), or retry implicitly on the next iteration (the oracle returns the same unit again because its findings file is still absent). They differ observably — inline retry never re-reads cycle state between attempts and needs its own attempt counter keyed on `(kind, id)` surviving across iterations; oracle-driven retry cannot bound attempts at all for kinds the oracle re-derives. The concurrent case is worse: if two of five `review-role` siblings fail, the spec does not say whether the driver retries them together, retries them one at a time, or waits for the next iteration.
suggestion: Add a retry step to §3.1's loop and name where the attempt counter lives (in-memory for the run, keyed `(kind, id)`, reset when the unit's predicate is satisfied). State whether the driver retries failed siblings within the same iteration and whether a retried sibling runs concurrently with the surviving ones, and say that a unit that exhausts its attempts stops the run only after in-flight siblings finish (matching §3.4's cap rule).

finding: §3.4 admits overshoot for exactly two caps — "a run can overshoot its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration" — but the same "caps are evaluated between iterations only" rule applies to `run_max_units`, and §3.3 spawns role units in parallel ("bounded by the number of active roles for the phase"). An iteration that spawns five role units when two remain under `run_max_units` overshoots the unit cap by three, which the overshoot sentence does not permit and the `cap-units` row ("Spawned children reached `run_max_units`") does not describe.
suggestion: Either add `run_max_units` to the overshoot sentence ("wall-clock, budget and unit caps", noting the unit overshoot is bounded by the phase's role count), or state that the driver truncates a parallel role batch to the remaining unit budget — and say which, since §10.5 test 33 pins all three unit counters to the same number.

finding: Round 7's machine surface sentence — "`next_units`, `round` and `phase` are the whole machine surface: the driver parses those three and nothing else" — is contradicted by two unchanged requirements. §3.5 requires `tp run --status` to carry `spec_coverage_clean_rounds`, `role_streaks` and `divergence` "verbatim from `tp audit --status`", which is the driver parsing a fourth, fifth and sixth key from another command's JSON; and §4.1's own next paragraph relies on `next_action.summary` to name what a `no-units` phase is waiting for.
suggestion: Scope the claim to the decision surface: "the driver's *control* decisions read only `next_units`, `round` and `phase`; §3.5's status passthrough copies additional fields without deciding on them." That preserves the anti-prose-parsing intent while staying true to §3.5.

finding: "tp records a `last_failure` object" names no component, but the two trigger conditions live on opposite sides of the process boundary: "exits non-zero" is only observable to the driver, while "closes with a failed quality gate" happens inside a child's own `tp done`. An implementer must therefore write the same file from two code paths without being told, and the file's single-object rule then races: concurrent role siblings that both fail write in nondeterministic order, so which failure survives is unspecified — unlike §5.2, which explicitly resolves the same collision for escalation records by reporting the lowest `seq`.
suggestion: Say which component writes `last_failure` in each case (the driver on a failed attempt; `tp done` itself on a gate failure, so it survives outside a run too), and resolve the concurrent case on the same terms as §5.2 — e.g. when one iteration produces several failures, the lowest `seq` is the one recorded. State whether a gate failure inside a child that the driver then also counts as a failed attempt writes the record once or twice.

finding: §4.2 says tp records `last_failure` "when a unit exits non-zero, or closes with a failed quality gate", keyed by `{unit_kind, unit_id}`. The exit-code case is observed by the driver, but the gate case is observed inside the child by `tp done`, which can only take kind and id from `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID`. §4.2 never says what a gate failure outside a run does — write a record with empty kind and id (which then never clears, since clearing requires a `(unit_kind, unit_id)` match), or write nothing. §5.2 defines the analogous outside-a-run case for `tp escalate` explicitly, so the omission here is an inconsistency in how the spec treats the same condition.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §4.2: outside a run (`TP_RUN_DIR`/`TP_UNIT_KIND` unset) a failed gate writes no `last_failure` — or defines the record's kind/id fallback and its clearing rule. Mirror it in §10.3 test 23.

finding: The table row fences "`tp set --workflow run_max_*=` above the resolved value", but the prose immediately after justifies the fence for two fields only ("a unit that could raise `run_max_units` or `run_max_wall_clock_seconds` could run itself indefinitely"), and §7 defines five `run_max_*` fields. Whether `run_max_budget_usd`, `run_max_unit_budget_usd` and `run_max_unit_retries` are fenced is left to the implementer, and the cases genuinely differ: raising `run_max_unit_retries` extends the run the same way, while raising `run_max_unit_budget_usd` spends more without extending it. Test 19's "each of the four user-only operations" counts table rows, so it does not settle which fields the fourth row covers.
suggestion: Enumerate the fenced fields literally instead of globbing — state that all five `run_max_*` fields plus `review_max_rounds`, `audit_max_rounds`, `runner` and `notify_cmd` are fenced, or name the exceptions and why raising them cannot manufacture convergence.

finding: §5.1 states that under `TP_UNATTENDED` "the env layer of §7's precedence is ignored for every fenced field" and that `runner` is fenced most strictly — "a unit cannot set them at all, at any layer". §3.2.1 states `TP_RUNNER` "outranks every layer of §7's precedence, including a CLI flag". Children inherit the driver's environment, so in exactly the configuration the tests use (a driver pinned with `TP_RUNNER`, children stamped `TP_UNATTENDED=1`) two sections give opposite answers for how a child's tp process resolves `runner`, and neither section names the other as the exception.
suggestion: State the resolution explicitly in one place — most plausibly that `TP_RUNNER` outranks every §7 layer *and* is exempt from the §5.1 env fence because only the driver process consults it, with the fence applying to `tp set --workflow runner=` and to config layers. §10.5 test 40 should then assert the exemption rather than leaving it inferred.

finding: The plugin preflight has no host. §6.1 requires that "if `tp` is absent from `PATH` or older than `0.35.0`, it fails with the install command rather than degrading quietly", but §6.2's table declares exactly three hooks — `SessionStart`, `PreToolUse`, `Stop` — and none of them is a preflight, so there is no component to implement this in. The failure channel is undefined too: whether it blocks the session, writes to stderr, or injects context, and what exit code it uses — and §6.4 requires every shipped hook to declare a 10-second timeout, which a preflight would need. Relatedly, the `SessionStart` hook's payload is `tp resume --compact`, whose own failure (no task file discovered, tp missing) has no specified handling.
suggestion: Assign the preflight to a named hook (the simplest is the `SessionStart` hook doing the version check before emitting `tp resume --compact`), and say what it emits on failure and on a `tp resume` that exits non-zero — e.g. inject a one-line notice naming the install command and exit 0, so a missing or stale binary never blocks the session silently.

finding: §6.1's preflight is normative — "if `tp` is absent from `PATH` or older than `0.35.0`, it fails with the install command rather than degrading quietly. The minimum is `plugin.json`'s own version, compared against `tp --version`" — but §10.4's four tests cover only `claude plugin validate`, the `PreToolUse` deny, the Stop hook and `TP_ROUND_DIR` emission. No test exercises the absent-binary or older-version branch, and the comparison rule (exact string? semver ordering? prerelease tags?) is unpinned, so two engineers disagree on whether `0.35.0-rc1` passes.
suggestion: Add a §10.4 test covering both preflight branches with a stubbed `tp --version`, and state in §6.1 that the comparison is semver ordering with prereleases below the release.

finding: Round 7 made the `claude` template append `["--agent", "<name>"]` per unit kind, which contradicts the paragraph directly under it: "A runner that cannot load a plugin gets no agent definitions, and the unit runs without them." With the flag hard-appended, a host without the plugin does not run the unit without the agent — `--agent tp-implementer` names an agent that does not exist, and the child fails at launch, turning every unit into a unit failure. §3.2.1's enumeration of the template's args is also now incomplete (it lists only the base args plus the budget pair) and says nothing about where the agent pair sits relative to the budget pair.
suggestion: State the degradation rule concretely: either the append is conditional on the agent definitions being present/resolvable, or the graceful-degradation sentence is withdrawn and a missing plugin is declared a preflight failure alongside §6.1's version check. Either way, add the agent pair to §3.2.1's args enumeration with its append order, and have test 44 cover the no-plugin path.

finding: "Under `--compact`, `stop_reason` and the cap totals survive; per-unit rows and log paths are stripped" sits in §7 immediately after a sentence about `tp config --resolved`/`--extract`/`tp validate --project`, but its subject matter (per-unit rows, log paths) belongs to `tp run --status` (§3.5). Which command's `--compact` is being specified is not pinned, and no test in §10 covers it at all, so the claim is both ambiguous and unverified.
suggestion: Move the sentence to §3.5, name the command (`tp run --status --compact`), and add a numbered test asserting the surviving and stripped keys.

finding: §3.2 says `runner` "takes one of three shapes: a built-in template name, a runner object, or a map from unit kind to either of those with a `default` key", and §3.2's whole per-kind-model argument depends on the third shape. §7's table gives `runner` the range "Built-in name or object" — two shapes — and §7 then says `tp config --resolved`, `tp config --extract` and `tp validate --project` cover the new fields "on the same terms as every existing workflow field". Validated against §7's stated range, the documented per-kind map is a validation error.
suggestion: Extend §7's Range cell for `runner` to "Built-in name, object, or per-kind map with `default`", and state in §7 that `tp validate --project` accepts all three shapes and rejects a map missing `default` as the usage error §3.2 already names.

finding: §7 puts the new fields under the precedence "CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in" and test 16 asserts "a CLI flag beats a task override", but no CLI flag is named anywhere in the spec for any of the seven fields — `tp run`'s documented surface is only `[spec]`, `--file`, `--status` and `--dry-run`. The implementer must invent the flag names, and the test cannot be written against the spec. The same hole covers `notify_cmd`: it is "read from `.tp/local.json` only", but no command is named that writes it there, so there is no specified way for an operator to configure the field §5.2 requires — while §5.1 simultaneously demands that a unit be refused when it tries to set it "at any layer".
suggestion: List the `tp run` flags for each field (e.g. `--max-units`, `--max-wall-clock-seconds`, `--max-budget-usd`, `--max-unit-budget-usd`, `--max-unit-retries`, `--runner`) and state whether they are run-scoped only or persist. Name the command that writes `notify_cmd` into `.tp/local.json` (or state that it is hand-edited by the operator and that no tp command writes it, which is what makes the §5.1 fence enforceable).

finding: `location_clusters` is the largest new payload this spec adds to an agent-facing command (`tp review --merge` and `--status`), yet it is explicitly reporting-only: convergence arithmetic, the stored `clean` flag and the `--status --check` exit code are all unchanged, so no machine branch reads it. On the spec's own measurement it would emit an entry for each of ~63 clustered locations, each carrying `{location, roles[], severities[], count}` — every byte of it parsed by the agent that reads merge output, feeding a judgement only a human makes. §7 states a `--compact` rule for the run state (per-unit rows and log paths stripped) but neither §8a nor §7 states one for `location_clusters` or for `inputs`, so the default is that a driver pays for the whole cluster table on every merge.
suggestion: State the `--compact` rule for §8a's new payloads in §8a itself: under `--compact`, strip `location_clusters` entirely (or reduce it to a single count of clustered locations) and keep `inputs`, which does feed the exit-code branch. Add the assertion to test 28 so the stripping is pinned rather than left to the implementer.

finding: §8a's round-7 rewrite asserts "exit 2 means uniformly 'tp did not run the request'" while withdrawing the subdivision. But §5.2's `tp escalate` exits 2 *after* running the request and performing a durable write (the escalation record), and §5.1's refusals exit 2 after tp evaluated the request and declined it. The uniform gloss is therefore false for at least one command that this same spec introduces, which weakens the very claim the withdrawal was meant to make defensible.
suggestion: Restate the invariant as what the driver may conclude rather than as a description of tp's internal handling: exit 2 means "do not treat this as work completed; stop and hand the log to a human", with the escalation record (§5.2) as the one artifact that reclassifies the stop. That keeps the no-subdivision decision without claiming something `tp escalate` contradicts.

finding: Test 14 says `tp run --status` "reports an in-flight run, a converged run and each stopped run", which reads as a history over multiple runs. §3.5 keeps exactly one file per task file (`.tp/run-<base>.json`) and says `--status` prints "the current or last run", with totals restarting at zero on a new run — no run history exists to enumerate.
suggestion: Reword test 14 as "reports an in-flight run, a converged run, and a run stopped for each `stop_reason`", so it is a matrix over stop reasons rather than over retained runs.

finding: Test 26 still reads "the Stop hook ... does block one that ended with neither its durable write nor a record" in generic unit terms, while §6.2's round-7 repair narrowed the hook to `TP_UNIT_KIND` ending in `-role` and moved every other kind's predicate to the driver. Read literally, test 26 asks for a hook that blocks a non-role unit, which §6.2 forbids.
suggestion: Qualify test 26 to role units, and add a clause asserting the hook does *not* fire for a non-role kind, so the narrowing is pinned rather than left implicit.

finding: §10.6 says "The `.tp/.gitignore` fixture gains three entries", but §10.2 test 15 asserts four newly ignored paths — `.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/` and `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json` — and §3.1 additionally introduces `.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock`. The two test sections pin different fixture sizes for the same file.
suggestion: State the exact entry list once (in §10.2 test 15) and have §10.6 refer to it rather than restating a count; if one glob is intended to cover two of the paths, say which.

finding: Of the eight variables every child is spawned with, `TP_ROUND` is the only one no section names a consumer for. `TP_RUN_DIR`/`TP_UNIT_SEQ` are read by escalation (§5.2), `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID`/`TP_ROUND_DIR` by the Stop hook and the agent allowlists (§6.2, §6.3), `TP_FILE` by the child's own tp calls, `TP_RUN_ID` by `notify_cmd`. `TP_ROUND` is used only as a substitution *into* `TP_ROUND_DIR` (`.tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND`), from which it is recoverable, so it is a value the driver exports and nothing documented reads back. Test 37 then pins all eight, which makes an unused knob permanent.
suggestion: Either name the consumer that needs the bare round number (and say so in §3.1), or drop `TP_ROUND` from the exported set and reduce test 37 to seven variables — a child that needs the round reads the `-r<N>` suffix of `TP_ROUND_DIR`.

finding: §3.2 gives `runner` three legal shapes — a built-in template name, a runner object, or a per-kind map with a mandatory `default` key — but §7's table, which is what `tp validate --project` and `tp config --resolved` are built from ("cover the new fields on the same terms as every existing workflow field"), records the range as "Built-in name or object". A validator written from §7 rejects the per-kind map that §3.2 makes a first-class capability, and §10 has no test asserting the map validates or that a map missing `default` is the documented usage error.
suggestion: Extend §7's range cell to "Built-in name, runner object, or per-kind map with `default`", and add a test asserting `tp validate --project` accepts all three shapes and rejects a map without `default` as exit 2.
